Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be
  effectively used for image super-resolution tasks.  However, the adversarial training
  process is unstable and the resulting models are difficult to train and produce
  inconsistent results.  In this work, we introduce a new training approach that
  eliminates the adversarial component by deriving an explicit super-resolution loss
  function from the latent variable distribution.  This approach, known as AutoSR,
  allows the model to be trained using only a single network, resulting in improved
  training stability and efficiency.  Our experiments on public datasets demonstrate
  that AutoSR outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in image super-resolution.

We tackle this question by applying a well-established framework from economics, specifically the revealed preference theory, to the analysis of algorithmic social bias.  This approach enables us to identify the underlying preferences that a learning model is implicitly capturing.  We then apply this framework to a variety of machine learning tasks, including classification, ranking, and regression, to examine the limitations of existing metric-based approaches in detecting social bias.  Our findings highlight the inefficiency of current methods in classification and ranking, and the inadequacy of the "equal average treatment effect" criterion in regression.  Moreover, our analysis uncovers a fundamental issue with the majority of social bias metrics, which is their inability to account for the underlying preferences that a learning model is implicitly capturing.  As a result, these metrics may yield misleading assessments of social bias.  To illustrate this, we provide a proof of concept using a simple yet effective algorithm that can fool current metric-based approaches.

(OOD) data is a crucial aspect of
  practical Deep Learning applications.  However, most OOD detection methods
  rely on training data and fail to identify OOD data when the input
  distribution shifts from that of the training data.  This research proposes
  a novel framework that combines domain adaptation and OOD detection to
  develop a method capable of detecting OOD data in real-world scenarios.  At
  the heart of this framework is a new Out-of-Domain (OOD) Detection Module
  (ODM) that leverages a discriminator to classify inputs as either In-Domain
  (ID) or OOD.  To ensure the ODM's robustness, it is trained on a dataset
  that is uncorrelated with the training data but shares the same labels.  To
  address the issue of domain shift from the training data to real-world
  scenarios, the proposed framework employs a Domain Adaptation Module (DAM)
  to adapt the ODM to the ID and OOD distributions encountered in the
  real-world scenario.  The framework is evaluated on multiple OOD detection
  benchmarks and demonstrates significant improvements in OOD detection
  performance compared to existing methods.

A key challenge in streaming algorithms is to minimize space usage while maintaining accuracy, but this becomes even more difficult when trying to reduce space while achieving adversarial robustness.  In this paper, we introduce a general framework for designing space-efficient robust estimators for linear functions, which can be applied to a wide range of problems.  Our approach is based on the concept of a robust base estimator, which is a randomized algorithm that produces an unbiased estimate of a target value with constant success probability and bounded space usage.  By combining multiple robust base estimators, we can create an estimator that is both adversarially robust and has a success probability that approaches one.  Our framework is shown to be effective in solving several important problems, including mean estimation, covariance estimation, and matrix completion.  Our framework is also shown to be optimal in terms of space usage for certain problems, and we provide new space-efficient robust algorithms for several important problems.

Our approach yields clear insights into the Casimir energy's relationship to the stress-energy of quantum fields, even in complex scenarios involving interacting fields and curved spacetime.  We demonstrate that the expectation value of the field's density of states, multiplied by the thermal energy, equals the Casimir energy.  This connection is established through the spectral properties of the field and is applicable to a wide range of situations.  Our derivation also considers the renormalization process and its impact on the Casimir energy.  As an illustration, we apply our theory to scalar fields in a finite one-dimensional box, obtaining an exact formula for the Casimir energy.  This result is then extended to include interactions and gravitational effects.  We further explore the implications of our theory for the Casimir effect in more complex scenarios, such as scalar fields with self-interactions in anti-de Sitter space.  Our findings provide a solid foundation for understanding the Casimir effect in a wide range of scenarios, and may have important applications in theoretical physics and cosmology.

As these beams collide, they generate an oblique shock, which serves as a model for the interaction between solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere.  The interaction of these counter-streaming plasma beams was simulated using a one-dimensional, hybrid code, which treats ions as particles and simulates the electromagnetic fields using Maxwell's equations.  The simulation revealed that oblique shocks exhibit a unique property: ions that are reflected from the shock front can become trapped in a region of high energy, forming a "boiling" effect.  This phenomenon is a result of the ions' phase-space mixing and can be compared to a thermalization process.  The "boiling" effect is most pronounced at shock angles of approximately 50-60 degrees, which is the most common angle of interaction between solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere.  The "boiling" effect can also explain the formation of diffuse cosmic rays in space.

  Although significant advancements have been made in code summarization,

  To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach called MetaCodeSum,

  To enhance the accuracy of summaries, MetaCodeSum utilizes a multi-task attention mechanism that captures contextual information from neighboring code.

examine the performance of a multi-antenna user in an OFDM-based wireless network, where the network is affected by a specific type of signal distortion known as subcarrier spacing mismatch. This mismatch occurs when there is a discrepancy in the synchronization of transceivers with respect to subcarrier spacing. To address this issue, we first develop a mathematical model that accurately represents the distorted signals, and then derive an analytical expression for the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) of the user's desired signal. This model is then used to derive closed-form expressions for key performance metrics, including SINR, symbol error rate (SER), and achievable data rate. To validate our theoretical findings, we provide numerical results that demonstrate the accuracy of our expressions and illustrate the impact of subcarrier spacing mismatch on performance. Furthermore, we also investigate the impact of subcarrier spacing mismatch on the achievable data rate and propose a low-complexity, discrete optimization algorithm to maximize the data rate under limited power constraints.

  Unlike traditional supervised learning, our method incorporates unlabeled images

  To this end, we introduce a new framework that combines contrastive learning
  with a knowledge distillation technique.
  The framework uses a teacher-student network setup, where the student network
  is trained on both labeled and unlabeled data, while the teacher network is
  trained solely on the limited labeled data.
  The two networks are then aligned through a contrastive learning process,
  which encourages the network to produce similar segmentation maps for
  semantically similar images.
  The student network is then refined using a knowledge distillation loss,
  which forces it to mimic the teacher network's predictions.

In this study, we investigate the behavior of multiple layers in a single collapsing object, considering various configurations of Lorentz factors and energy densities.  We also explore the effects of different distribution types, including broken power laws, Gaussian profiles, and top-hat shapes.  Our findings reveal that the outermost layer's Lorentz factor accurately reflects the behavior of the entire system, regardless of its configuration.  However, discrepancies arise when the outermost layer contains only low-energy particles.  In such cases, the inner layers exhibit a steeper decline in the Lorentz factor than predicted by the inverse of the energy density.  This discrepancy can be rectified by introducing an additional dissipation layer in the outflow's configuration.  Our research holds significant implications for the interpretation of multi-wavelength afterglows in GRB observations, particularly in cases where the dissipation occurs within a single collapsing object.

of stochastic control problems where the underlying dynamics are influenced by fast periodic fluctuations.  We prove that as the period approaches zero, the corresponding control problems converge to a homogenized limit.  Under reasonable assumptions, we also demonstrate that a solution to the homogenized equation can be obtained by perturbing the periodic solution to a set of nearby equations as the fast scale parameter increases.  We achieve this result by applying a change of variables to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, and verifying that the transformed function satisfies the conditions of viscosity solutions.  This provides an alternative proof of previously established homogenization results and offers new insights into the relationship between the homogenized and original problems.

A critical aspect of this situation is the need to make a series of interrelated choices, where each decision impacts the available options for future actions.  In this study, we present a novel approach to modeling such scenarios, where we examine the problem of making optimal decisions under uncertainty, given a limited understanding of the underlying dynamics.  We represent this problem using a framework that includes a series of interconnected states, where each action taken leads to a change in the future actions available.  We then develop an algorithm capable of efficiently handling this complex problem, where we demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of simulations.  We also explore the implications of this approach in the context of public health policy, where we apply it to a hypothetical scenario of pandemic response.  We present the results of this application, where we compare the optimal strategy to our model with the outcomes of a real-world policy decision.  We find that our model provides valuable insights into the complexities of pandemic response, where we demonstrate that the optimal strategy differs significantly from the policy decision made in the hypothetical scenario.  We also find that our model can be used to evaluate the potential consequences of different policy decisions, where we demonstrate that the results of this evaluation can inform future policy decisions.  We conclude that our approach provides a valuable tool for analyzing complex decision-making scenarios, where we demonstrate that our approach can be used to inform policy decisions in the context of pandemic response.

growing interest in using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for real-time rendering of scenes. 3DGS has demonstrated its potential by outperforming Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) in various benchmarks. However, 3DGS lacks an explicit scene representation, which makes it challenging to optimize and update efficiently. This paper introduces a novel optimization technique that leverages the differentiability of the rasterization process to update 2D Gaussian features directly via the Jacobian-vector product, which is a significant advancement that enables efficient optimization and updates of 3D Gaussian splatting. This technique is a crucial enabler for applications such as dynamic scene reconstruction and object insertion. We validate our approach by developing two new techniques for dynamic scene reconstruction and object insertion, which allow for the efficient and accurate updates of 3D Gaussian splatting in real-time.

  investigate the effect of the interaction strength on the late-time value of

, the Lorentz transformation is a fundamental concept that plays a crucial role.  Historically, Lorentz derived this transformation based on the ether theory's assumptions, with Lorentz being the first to obtain it.  However, his derivation relied on solving Maxwell's equations, which are part of the Special Theory of Relativity, resulting in a circular reasoning process.  In an attempt to break this cycle, Lorentz used the Maxwell equations that were already consistent with his final conclusion.  In this study, we derive the Lorentz transformation from Maxwell's equations without any preconceived notions about the relationship between space and time, with the outcome being that the transformation is found to be equivalent to Lorentz's original conclusion.  In this derivation, we also establish that time is an intrinsic property of any physical process, which is a fundamental aspect of the universe.

  mechanism in the ViT, viewing it as a method for aligning local visual

  To address these challenges, we propose a self-attention alternative that
  incorporates an external supervision signal to enhance semantic

  equitable patch representation.

  importance of the alignment objective and the quality of the aligned
  representations.
  Through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, our results
  demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed improvements in enhancing
  visual representation learning based on the ViT.

  WW, ZZ, $\gamma\gamma$, and $b\bar{b}$ decay channels, across various
  differential cross-sections and total cross-sections.  We extract the Higgs
  boson's coupling to vector bosons, as well as other particles, in terms of

The top quark's short lifetime prevents it from being directly detected in B decay experiments, necessitating an indirect approach through analyzing the photon spectrum. The top quark's production and decay result in a characteristic displacement between the B and decay points, which can be detected experimentally. The interference between the direct and penguin diagrams in B->X_{s}gamma allows for a precise determination of the B quark's momentum distribution, which is essential for long-distance B meson formation. The top quark's lifetime and formation length provide crucial constraints on the coherence between B and top wave packets. The top quark's formation time is comparable to its lifetime, which is a crucial factor in the interference between the direct and penguin diagrams. The formation time of the top quark can be estimated using the Yennie-Jost-Sandars model, which predicts a formation time of approximately 5*10^{-25}s. The formation time of the B meson is estimated to be approximately 1 fm/c, which is a crucial factor in the interference between the B and top wave packets. The interference between the B and top wave packets is crucial for the precision of the B->X_{s}gamma decay measurements.

This method trains a neural network to approximate the optimal solution to a problem by leveraging the gradient information of the objective function and the Lagrangian, which is a combination of the objective and the constraints.  The proposed approach, which we call LagrangeNet, utilizes a neural network to model the Lagrangian, which is a function of the variables and the Lagrange multipliers.  The network is then optimized using a custom loss function that takes into account the gradient information of the objective function and the constraints.  The Lagrange multipliers are updated using a gradient-based update rule that is similar to the one used in gradient descent methods.  The proposed approach is demonstrated on a range of optimization problems, including the design of an antenna array, the optimization of a mechanical structure, and a set of benchmark problems.  The results show that LagrangeNet can effectively find high-quality solutions to complex optimization problems.

  malicious miners who generate blocks containing conflicting transactions.  We
  show that, if a sufficient number of miners publish blocks with conflicting
  transactions, the probability of the blockchain accepting both conflicting
  transactions becomes significant.  This finding is surprising because the
  ability to publish a conflicting block does not necessarily grant the ability
  to force the entire blockchain to accept that block.  Our analysis is
  conducted within the context of Bitcoin and several transaction-based
  blockchain protocols.  We also develop a measure called "conflicting power" to
  quantify the ability of an adversary to publish conflicting blocks and provide
  theoretical bounds for this measure under various assumptions.  Our results
  indicate that an adversary who can control a substantial amount of the network
  hashing power can potentially publish conflicting blocks at a high rate.

sum of squares (SOS) offer a
  computationally efficient and reliable way to find solutions to polynomial
  optimization problems.  However, the quality of the solutions obtained by SOS
  methods can vary significantly.  In this research, we explore the performance of
  semidefinite programming relaxations in solving the minimum $k$-cut problem.  We
  show that the quality of the SOS solutions is heavily influenced by the size of
  SOS certificates.  Specifically, we prove that the size of the smallest degree-$d$
  SOS certificate that lower bounds the degree-$d$ SOS value by the true value of
  the minimum $k$-cut is upper bounded by $O(k^2)$, and this bound is tight.  We
  also show that the degree of the SOS relaxation is a critical factor in the
  performance of the method.  In particular, we show that if the SOS certificate
  has a small degree, then the solution to the SOS relaxation is an integer
  solution, and if the SOS relaxation has a high degree, then the solution can be
  arbitrarily far from the optimal solution of the minimum $k$-cut problem.  We
  also provide a new, concise proof for a recent result that showed that if the SOS
  relaxation has a degree of $k-1$, then it can represent any feasible semialgebraic
  $k$-cut partition

the intergalactic medium poses a significant challenge to the standard cosmological model. The model predicts that the probability of finding regions with high density on the scale of hundreds of Mpc is extremely low, which contradicts the observations of large scale magnetic fields. This study proposes a novel explanation for these fields by suggesting that they are contained within domain walls, which are predicted to form as a result of symmetry breaking phase transitions in the early universe. The magnetic fields within these domain walls are proposed to be generated by the interaction between the Higgs and axion fields, which are believed to exist in the universe. The study derives the necessary conditions for the formation of these domain walls and estimates their contribution to the cosmic microwave background anisotropies. The results of this study suggest that the proposed model is consistent with the observations of large scale magnetic fields and can provide a novel probe of the physics of the early universe.

hidden variable models, including the de Broglie-Bohm theory, cannot account for the observed correlations in the experiment conducted by Hanson et al. (2007).  This experiment involved the detection of entangled electrons in separate locations, where the measurement of each electron's spin influenced the result of a prior measurement of its orbital angular momentum.  A key aspect of the experiment was that the measurement of the first particle's spin was not independent of the measurement of its previous angular momentum, violating the assumption of local measurement independence.  We provide a detailed analysis of the experiment and derive a specific inequality that is violated by the observed results.  The violation of this inequality indicates that nonlocal hidden variable models, which include the Bohmian mechanics, cannot explain the observed correlations in the experiment.  The significance of this finding is that it shows the entanglement of the electrons' spin and orbital degrees of freedom in the experiment cannot be explained by nonlocal hidden variable models that satisfy the condition of measurement independence.

The Standard Model's predicted value for the neutron EDM is extremely small, making it insufficient to explain observed CP violation in nature.  New sources of CP violation are necessary to account for phenomena such as baryon asymmetry. , the decay of heavy neutral Higgs bosons into pairs of light neutral Higgs bosons is an important process.  In this study, we investigate the potential production of three Higgs bosons at the Large Hadron Collider through the process of proton-proton collisions.  We focus on the scenario where one of the three Higgs bosons decays into a pair of bottom quarks and the other two decay into leptons and neutrinos via $Z$ bosons. -level atom interacting with a single-mode cavity field is a widely studied model in quantum optics.  The Jay Cummings Hamiltonian's behavior is characterized by two main phenomena: a weak atom-field interaction results in an energy exchange known as Rabi oscillation, while a stronger interaction leads to a redistribution of energy between the atom and field, called "collapse and revival".  In this study, we investigate the system's dynamics in a phase space representation, utilizing the Wigner function to analyze its properties.  Our findings reveal that short-time atom-field interactions produce interference patterns, whereas longer interaction times lead to the emergence of Rabi oscillations distinguishable by alternating dark and bright regions.  Furthermore, we find that the system's "collapse and revival" phenomenon manifests as the formation of distinct clusters in phase space, which evolve over time.

^2/2m + V(x)$ for a non-relativistic particle fails to accurately describe the behavior of an electron in the vicinity of its nucleus.  The Dirac equation, however, provides a more suitable framework for this situation.  By applying the positive energy projection operator to the Dirac Hamiltonian, a four-component effective Schrödinger equation is obtained.  A novel approach is then introduced to derive the corresponding classical limit of this effective equation, resulting in the identification of the classical potential energy as the expectation value of the Dirac potential operator.  Furthermore, the approach yields a classical kinetic energy that differs from the expected $p^2/2m$ form.  A novel semi-kinetic potential is therefore defined to account for this discrepancy.  A detailed analysis of this potential is provided, along with an examination of its relation to the Zitterbewegung phenomenon.

in astrophysical and geophysical flows, researchers rely on Reynolds-averaged equations, which require the determination of turbulent fluxes.  A common approach to achieve this is through linear closure methods, such as the Reynolds stress closure, that model turbulent fluxes based on mean flow gradients.  A key aspect of these methods is to formulate closure relations that are consistent with fundamental physical principles, including the Reynolds transport theorem.  This paper presents a novel approach to derive such a closed system of equations for turbulent transport by utilizing the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes formulation and applying a rigorous mathematical technique to decouple turbulent and mean flow components.  This approach yields a set of closed equations that describe turbulent transport, which can be used to derive integral balances for turbulent kinetic energy and its dissipation rate, as well as mean flow quantities.  Furthermore, this framework enables the development of physically consistent closure relations, which can be used to model turbulent transport in complex flows.

  origin of FRBs remains a subject of debate, with multiple theories proposed
  to explain their formation.  In this study, we propose a novel method to
  investigate the origins of FRBs by analyzing their electromagnetic counterparts
  and utilizing gravitational wave detectors to precisely locate FRB sources.
  By combining these approaches, we can determine the distance, redshift, and
  sky position of gravitational wave events, which in turn allows us to narrow
  down the search area for their associated FRBs.  By applying this method to
  GW190814, we identified a potential FRB counterpart located approximately
  130 million parsecs away from the FRB source, which is consistent with the
  estimated distance of the gravitational wave event.

finite automata is an
  ongoing research topic in theoretical computer science.  This research is
  motivated by the desire to understand the fundamental capabilities of
  memory-constrained computational systems.  In this paper, we investigate
  deterministic two-way finite state transducers, which are capable of reading
  input in both directions.  We focus on rational functions, which map strings
  to strings with certain pattern-based restrictions.  We establish that any
  function computable by a transducer with $m$ states and a rational language
  is contained within a specific set of functions characterized by the Myhill-
  Nerode equivalence of finite automata and expressed using regular expressions.
  This new upper bound is strictly more complex than previous findings for
  standard finite automata.  Additionally, we demonstrate that this upper
  bound is achievable with a specific class of functions that are computationally
  efficient to evaluate.

It is hypothesized that cells communicate through chemical signals to coordinate their placement within the tissue.  To investigate this, a model is proposed in which cells exchange information via a shared medium, influenced by local and non-local factors.   multiple stable states, which can be influenced by external factors such as solar
  activity and volcanic eruptions.  The occurrence of sudden, unexpected shifts
  from one state to another is possible, and this phenomenon is often
  misinterpreted as a change in the climate's tipping points.  Instead, we argue
  that the existing framework of climate change theory needs to be expanded to
  incorporate the dynamics of forced, dissipative systems.  We demonstrate that

  anticipate sudden, unexpected changes in the climate's behavior, and we provide
  examples of how this can be applied to real-world phenomena such as glacial
  cycles and abrupt climate changes.  We also discuss the limitations of using
  traditional methods to identify climate's tipping points, and we propose new
  metrics that can be used to detect the occurrence of sudden, unexpected changes
  in the climate's behavior.  This new framework can be used to develop more
  accurate models of climate dynamics, and to improve our ability to predict
  future climate changes.

  This question has been extensively studied in the field of quantum information,
  with various approaches involving multiple particles and complex systems.
  Here, we focus on a more straightforward scenario, involving a single photon
  interacting with a two-level atom.
  By analyzing the single-particle entanglement between the photon's polarization
  and the atom's energy state, we identify the conditions under which this
  entanglement occurs.
  We derive a clear criterion for this phenomenon and demonstrate that it can
  arise from distinct initial conditions.
  Through a mathematical model, we establish a calculable relationship between
  the time it takes for the system to become entangled and the interaction
  strength between the particles.
  We also explore the possibility of controlling the entanglement generation
  process by introducing an external magnetic field.
  Our findings provide a foundation for developing more sophisticated protocols
  for creating entangled states in quantum systems.

's spatial and temporal characteristics is highly sought after in areas like optical communications, quantum information processing, and biomedical imaging.  Nonlinear processes, such as four-wave mixing, are capable of achieving this modulation, but their effectiveness is limited by the need for phase matching and high optical power.  We present a new approach to four-wave mixing that doesn't require phase matching or high power.  Our method uses two low-power, counter-rotating circularly polarized beams to generate optical vortices in a highly non-linear medium.  The phase matching condition is met due to the interaction between the counter-rotating beams, which creates a standing wave pattern with a phase singularity.  The generated optical vortices have a controllable topological charge, which can be manipulated by adjusting the power ratio between the two input beams.  Our method is versatile and can be applied to various nonlinear processes, including four-wave mixing, stimulated Raman scattering, and optical Kerr effect.

However, FWI's computational demands pose significant challenges, particularly in the context of 3D modeling. To address this issue, we explore the potential of employing reduced order modeling (ROM) to accelerate FWI. By utilizing a set of precomputed basis functions, ROM enables us to represent the seismic wavefield with greater efficiency. In this study, we investigate the application of ROM to FWI, with a focus on data assimilation and waveform matching objectives. We utilize the singular value decomposition (SVD) and the singular value decomposition with random projections (SVD-RP) methods to generate the basis functions. Our results demonstrate that SVD-RP offers a more efficient and accurate acceleration of FWI compared to SVD, particularly in data-driven workflows. Furthermore, we find that waveform-matching objectives provide greater acceleration than data-assimilation objectives, particularly in the context of the pre-stack wavefield. Our findings have significant implications for the development of efficient FWI algorithms, particularly in the context of 3D modeling.

is whether a model's
  vulnerability to adversarial attacks can be mathematically bounded by its
  inherent properties.  A recent study by Finlay et al. (2020) demonstrated that
  a model's susceptibility to adversarial attacks is intrinsically tied to its
  Lipschitz constant.  However, this relationship is limited to models with
  input-output Lipschitz continuity, which is a rare occurrence in practice.  In
  this paper, we argue that a more applicable metric is local sensitivity, which
  quantifies the maximum impact of a unit perturbation on the model's output.  We
  establish a direct connection between local sensitivity and adversarial
  accuracy, which holds for a broader range of models than the input-output Lipschitz
  continuity.  We validate our findings through experiments on various models,
  including deep neural networks, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees,
  which reveal that local sensitivity serves as a more reliable indicator of
  adversarial robustness than the Lipschitz constant.  Furthermore, we show that
  models can be optimized to minimize local sensitivity, which leads to a notable
  improvement in their adversarial accuracy.

ology of a novel dark matter candidate,
  a complex dark scalar field that carries a global $U(1)_D$ charge.  In order to
  stabilize this dark scalar field, we introduce a dark sector consisting of a
  dark photon and a dark photon collider.  The dark photon can decay into dark
  matter, which can then decay back into a dark photon and a dark matter particle.
  This decay chain can be probed in a variety of experiments, including dark
  matter direct detection experiments, beam dump experiments, and collider
  experiments.  In this work, we analyze the decay of the dark matter particle
  and its implications for dark matter direct detection experiments, as well as
  beam dump experiments and other low-energy experiments.  We also consider the
  implications of the dark matter decay for cosmology, in particular, the
  production of gravitational waves during inflation.  We show that the decay of
  the dark matter particle can have a significant impact on the production of
  gravitational waves during inflation, which can be probed by future gravitational
  wave detectors.

(LISA) will be a groundbreaking space-based gravitational wave detector, enabling the observation of cosmic events that current and future gravitational wave detectors cannot. LISA will be able to detect gravitational waves from low-frequency sources, providing a wealth of information about the universe. However, LISA's data will be challenging to analyze due to complex instrumental noise and the vast amount of data it will produce. To make sense of this data, we must accurately model the instrument's noise, which can be influenced by the LISA spacecraft's environment. We have developed a new method for noise modeling that uses a graph neural network to model the instrument's response to various noise sources, including light pressure, thermal fluctuations, and seismic vibrations. Our approach has been tested on LISA's testbeds and has shown significant improvements in noise modeling, particularly in the frequency range that LISA will be most sensitive to. Our results demonstrate that the graph neural network can model the instrument's noise more accurately than traditional methods, and can also identify previously unknown noise sources. Our work has important implications for the LISA mission, and could help ensure its success by providing more accurate data analysis and the ability to detect more cosmic events.

ospheric disturbance in the

  ionospheric enhancement was not a result of the spacecraft's interaction

  disturbance highlights the importance of considering the effects of solar

Quantum Monte Carlo simulations, a widely used computational method in physics, can be efficiently emulated on quantum computers through the development of tailored algorithms.  However, traditional quantum simulation algorithms fail to accurately replicate the results of quantum Monte Carlo simulations for certain Hamiltonians, such as those with non-stochastic Trotter terms. Our approach allows for a direct and fair comparison between quantum simulations and their quantum Monte Carlo counterparts, providing a valuable tool for evaluating the performance of quantum phase estimation algorithms.

In this context, a novel EH-CC system is proposed, in which an energy-harvesting secondary transmitter (STx) assists an information-transmitting primary user (Ptx) in a simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) network. The STx, which is powered by the Ptx's signal, is located between the Ptx and a primary receiver (Prx) and transmits both the Ptx's information and its own energy-generating signal to the Prx. To minimize the primary user's (PU) outage probability (OP) while maximizing the secondary user's (SU) energy efficiency (EE), an optimal spatial node distribution and optimal node placement are determined. To this end, a new SWIPT system model is introduced, in which the STx is randomly distributed in a two-dimensional area and the primary and secondary users are assumed to communicate via a Rayleigh fading channel. To analyze the performance of the proposed system, the primary user's end-to-end signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) cumulative distribution function (CDF) is derived, and the secondary user's energy efficiency is calculated. has gained significant

  decision-making problems.  However, the application of MARL in safety-
  critical domains poses serious risks, as unsafe exploration can lead to
  catastrophic outcomes.  To mitigate this issue, safety-constrained MARL
  approaches have been developed, but they often require extensive tuning
  and fail to guarantee safety.  In this paper, we introduce a novel framework
  called SafeCoRe, a safety-guaranteed continuous control MARL system that
  operates without manual tuning.  Our framework combines two key components:
  a conservative off-policy learning algorithm and a safety monitor that
  ensures agent safety.  The safety monitor is based on a conservative
  safety critic that predicts potential unsafe actions and intervenes to
  prevent them.  Our approach is evaluated on three challenging benchmarks,
  where it consistently outperforms existing safety-constrained MARL methods
  while requiring no manual tuning and guaranteeing safety.  Our code is
  publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhengyiwei/SafeCoRe}.

old.  Firstly, we provide a comprehensive
  overview of the existing research on the interplay between quantum information and
  black holes.  Secondly, we outline potential research directions in this field by
  examining the connection between quantum information and the thermodynamic
  properties of black holes.  To achieve this, we employ the gravitational path
  integral as a theoretical tool.  We discuss the application of the gravitational
  path integral in calculating the von Neumann entropy and the mutual information, as
  well as the spectrum of the graviton in anti-de Sitter space.  We also explore the
  possibility of using the gravitational path integral to compute the mutual
  information between the interior and exterior of an eternal black hole, which
  appears to be zero.  This result may be at odds with the expected unitary
  evolution of the system, which would imply that the eternal black hole cannot
  exist.  We also consider the possibility that the eternal black hole is merely an
  approximation that breaks down when the system is subjected to perturbations, which
  could lead to the formation of a singularity.  This possibility is supported by
  recent developments in the understanding of the gravitational path integral, which
  suggest that it can be used to compute the probabilities of distinct geometries,
  rather than just the amplitudes of individual geometries.

the Prisoner's Dilemma game, which is used as a model to study the evolution of cooperation. In a Prisoner's Dilemma game, two players are presented with two options: to cooperate or defect. The payoff for mutual cooperation is greater than that for mutual defection, but the payoff for defection is higher than that for cooperation. This creates a conflict between individual and collective interests. This study proposes a Prisoner's Dilemma game in which the payoff for cooperation is not fixed, but instead fluctuates over time according to a specific distribution. This modification allows for the analysis of the impact of cooperation variability on cooperative behavior in an evolutionary context. This study finds that the emergence of cooperation is influenced by the distribution of cooperation variability. Specifically, cooperation is more likely to evolve when the variability is distributed in a way that places more weight on higher payoff values. This study also compares the cooperative stability of different matching strategies, such as win-stay-lose-shift, anti-PD, and random matching, and finds that cooperation is more likely to evolve when players use the anti-PD strategy and match with those who have similar strategies.

Unlike its explicit counterpart, implicit models learn from unobserved data patterns and correlations, making them highly efficient in terms of memory usage and inference time.  However, the black-box nature of implicit models makes it difficult to interpret their inner workings and understand how they process information.  To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework for interpreting implicit neural networks that combines counterfactual analysis with counterfactual data visualization. By analyzing the specific-heat data, we found that the electronic specific-heat coefficient in this system is significantly influenced by the strength of the applied magnetic field. The concept of elastic 4D crystals was initially proposed in 2019,  and since then, experimental evidence supporting this theory has been  discovered in silicon crystals.  The dispersion relation of 4D crystals is  crucial for understanding their mechanical properties, and while the  mechanical behavior of 3D crystals can be explained by their point group  symmetries, the same approach is insufficient for 4D crystals.  The 4D crystal's mechanical properties depend on both its 4D and 3D sub-crystals, and to describe their symmetries, the use of the 5D hypercrystal is necessary.  The investigation of the 4D crystal's dispersion relation is carried  out using silicon as an example, and the results show that the  mechanical properties of 4D crystals can be understood through the  analysis of their phonon density.  The phonon density of states of 4D crystals  exhibits a unique feature, where the linear regime is absent, and the  quadratic regime is also not present.  The linear regime appears in 5D and higher dimensions, and the quadratic regime appears in 3D and 4D dimensions.  The results of this investigation provide a foundation for the search for  new 4D crystal materials.

behavior of a
  quantum particle in a one-dimensional lattice with a localized defect, in the
  presence of a strong driving force.  Our study reveals that a sudden increase in
  the driving force causes the particle to enter a rapid, periodic movement
  pattern, which is then interrupted by a period of irregular motion when the force
  is decreased.  This irregular motion is eventually replaced by a chaotic motion
  that is influenced by the rate at which the driving force is changed.  We also
  observe that the particle's motion is constrained by a maximum speed determined
  by the lattice structure, and this maximum speed can be altered by changing the
  localization of the defect.  We further show that the particle's motion can be
  described by a stability condition that is influenced by the lattice structure
  and the rate at which the driving force is changed.

accretion disks are among the most luminous and powerful objects in the universe.  The behavior of matter within these disks is primarily governed by the interaction between the disk and its magnetic field.  The magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) framework is the most comprehensive and accurate model for describing this interaction.  However, the vast majority of research on accretion disks has been theoretical or numerical in nature, with few observational studies.  The detection of broad, skewed Fe K$\alpha$ emission lines in the X-ray spectra of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and X-ray binaries (XRBs) provides compelling evidence for the presence of MHD effects in these systems.  The characteristics of these emission lines are highly sensitive to the properties of the inner disk, making them a valuable diagnostic tool for understanding the complex interplay between the disk and the black hole.  In this study, we utilize the general relativistic MHD code, HARM, to simulate the inner regions of a thin, steady, radiative accretion disk, and the resulting Fe K$\alpha$ emission lines.  By varying the black hole's spin and the magnetic field configuration, we explore the impact of these factors on the observed emission lines.  Our findings reveal that the black hole's spin has a significant influence on the shape of the Fe K$\alpha$ emission lines, with higher spin rates leading to more pronounced red wings. one infected individual in a population is known as $R_0$.  The concept of $R_0$ has been extensively applied in various fields, including epidemiology, social network theory, and even economics.  The term $R_0$ can be understood in multiple ways, including as the basic reproduction number, the branching number, the spectral radius of the adjacency matrix, or the Kolmogorov root of the transition matrix.  Although these definitions appear distinct, they are in fact equivalent under certain conditions, allowing for a unified perspective on $R_0$.  This unified view facilitates the extension of $R_0$ to scenarios where it may not be directly applicable, such as in directed graphs, weighted graphs, and bipartite graphs.  Moreover, this approach enables the derivation of relationships between the various definitions of $R_0$, including connections to the spectral and branching numbers of associated non-negative matrices.

  Bitcoin's redistributive effects, we utilize a novel approach that leverages

  suggest that the widespread adoption of digital currencies may exacerbate 
  income inequality, with the most significant effects being felt by the 
  wealthiest individuals.

was first proposed to address the challenge of reconstructing evolutionary histories from genomic data derived from multiple time points in infectious disease progression.  Given a set of evolutionary trees generated from genomic data across different time points, a Persistent Phylogeny is defined as a collection of interconnected trees that can be derived from a single overarching tree.  A key characteristic of persistent phylogenies is that the placement of any leaf node within any given tree remains consistent with its placement in the overarching tree.  This paper presents an algorithm capable of identifying all persistent phylogenies from a set of input trees, with a time complexity of O(n^2 * m^2 * m!), where n represents the total number of leaf nodes across all trees, and m denotes the maximum number of trees in the set.  A persistent phylogeny can be characterized as a set of edge-labeled trees that can be mapped onto a single overarching tree.  The edge labels correspond to the time points at which the corresponding edges appear in the input trees.  The problem of finding persistent phylogenies can be formulated as a constraint satisfaction problem, with the constraint that the relative ordering of any pair of leaf nodes must be maintained across all trees in the set.  The time complexity of our algorithm is a significant improvement over the previously best-known method, with a gain of a factor of n^2 * m^2 * m!.

learning models has led to a growing interest in knowledge distillation, a technique that allows a smaller student network to learn from a larger teacher network. This paper introduces a new knowledge distillation approach that leverages the student's ability to process intermediate network outputs, enabling it to learn from a wider range of information provided by the teacher. This new approach, Intermediate Feature Distillation (IFD), incorporates three types of knowledge from the teacher: target labels, softened activation distributions, and diverse intermediate feature representations. Experimental results on multiple datasets and network architectures show that IFD consistently outperforms traditional knowledge distillation methods, achieving a 0.64% improvement in top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with ResNet-50. Furthermore, IFD can be applied to various scenarios, including multi-task learning, domain adaptation, and continual learning, and can be combined with other techniques such as self-distillation and test-time augmentation.

Our experiments on two real-world datasets, Cora and Amazon-Computer Science, demonstrate the effectiveness of CF-GAT in providing high-quality explanations that are both human-interpretable and consistent with human intuition. depth sensors are becoming increasingly popular due to their low cost and high-speed performance.  However, they are prone to errors caused by manufacturing defects and environmental factors. event horizon of black holes has been confirmed through the detection of jets in active galactic nuclei and microquasars.  The detection of cyclotron lines in the X-ray spectra of accreting black holes and neutron stars would provide the first direct evidence of magnetic fields near the event horizon.  The discovery of a narrow absorption feature at 15.2 keV in the X-ray spectra of the black hole candidate XTE J1118+480, initially reported in 2007, was hypothesized to be a fundamental electron cyclotron line.  However, this interpretation was later disputed, and alternative explanations were proposed.  In this study, we re-examined the 2007 data and found that the absorption feature is indeed a fundamental electron cyclotron line, with the corresponding magnetic field strength being 3.5 x 10^12 G.  We also investigated the stability of this line in the Comptonization process and found that it remains identifiable in the X-ray spectra of XTE J1118+480.  The discovery of this cyclotron line in XTE J1118+480, along with a previous similar finding in the neutron star 4U 1254-690, provides the first direct evidence of magnetic fields in the vicinity of compact objects.

estimation of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) in a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), addressing an underappreciated challenge in GMM research.  Accurate knowledge of the FIM is crucial for numerous statistical tasks, such as hypothesis testing, confidence interval estimation, and risk minimization.  Unfortunately, existing methods for calculating the FIM in GMMs are either computationally inefficient, prone to numerical instability, or non-existent in many cases.  The paper presents a new, efficient approach for estimating the FIM that is both numerically stable and amenable to parallel computation.  The method leverages a previously unnoticed relationship between the Hessian of the log-likelihood function and the expected outer product of score functions, allowing for a simplified and computationally efficient calculation of the FIM.  The proposed method is demonstrated to be particularly useful in high-dimensional settings, where accurate confidence intervals for mixture weights are otherwise difficult to obtain.  The paper includes both simulated and real-world data experiments to showcase the effectiveness of the method.

layered perovskite
  compounds are intricately influenced by the interplay of strong electron
  correlations and structural characteristics.  We investigate the impact of
  lattice distortions on the magnetic behavior of Sr$_2$MmMnO$_6$ (Mm = Ca, Sr)
  by employing a combination of DFT+DMFT and analytical models.  The results
  demonstrate that the system can be effectively described as a two-band
  Hamiltonian, consisting of strongly localized $e_g$ electrons and itinerant
  $t_{2g}$ electrons, with the specific lattice symmetry playing a crucial role
  in determining the type of superexchange interaction between $e_g$ electrons.
  Our study reveals that Sr$_2$MmMnO$_6$ exhibits a rich phase diagram, with
  its magnetic properties governed by the competition between ferromagnetic and
  antiferromagnetic exchange interactions.  In particular, we find that the
  system undergoes a structural phase transition from a low-temperature
  ferromagnetic state to a high-temperature antiferromagnetic state, with the
  transition point shifting to lower temperatures as Ca is substituted for Sr.
  Our theoretical predictions are in line with experimental observations and
  provide valuable insights into the complex interplay of electron correlations
  and lattice distortions in quasi-two-dimensional layered perovskites.

  start of each episode, the agent faces an input and then takes actions across
  a sequence of time steps, receiving rewards and observations after each
  action.  Repetitive patterns emerge in the action sequences, and the reward
  at any given time step depends only on the action history since the most
  recent time step when the observation resets.  We propose a new algorithm,
  OSCR, that leverages this structure by treating actions tied to the same

  guarantees for its finite-horizon variant.  We demonstrate the effectiveness

  assemble furniture.

AMV) is a significant climate pattern that fluctuates on a decadal scale in the North Atlantic and has an impact on global climate. The study uses a two-box model to simulate the circulation and finds that the model can produce AMV with a period of around 50-70 years.  The research team discovered that the variability's period is primarily determined by the circulation's response to changes in salinity, and that the model's behavior can be influenced by changes in the mixed layer depth and the circulation's transport properties.   A key area of investigation is how deep neural networks learn to represent
  data, a process that is not fully understood.
  A significant aspect of this is how the architecture of deep networks
  influences their ability to capture meaningful data representations.
  A notable example is the disparity in representation performance between
  fully connected layers and convolutional layers in autoencoders.
  In this study, we investigate the underlying mechanisms of this difference.
  A key finding is that the nature of the layers' receptive fields plays a crucial
  role in determining their effectiveness at encoding data.
  A proposed solution, the adaptive convolutional layer, adapts convolution kernels
  to each input, bridging the gap between fully connected and convolutional layers.
  A surprising outcome is that applying adaptive convolutions to standard
  convolutional layers results in a substantial improvement in representation
  performance, outperforming even the equivalent fully connected design.

This phenomenon is a result of both permanent gravitational wave wedges and transient wedges, which can be observed by gravitational wave detectors. In this study, we investigate the ability of a detector to distinguish between these two types of wedges, using a maximum likelihood approach. We focus on a specific scenario: a detector observing a gravitational wave generated by a binary black hole merger, where the wedge is created by the merger's burst. We analyze the detectability of this memory wedge for various detector orientations and noise levels, and find that a detector with a high signal-to-noise ratio can clearly distinguish between the transient and permanent wedges. Conversely, a detector with a lower signal-to-noise ratio may struggle to detect the memory wedge. We also explore the potential of using gravitational wave memory to constrain cosmological parameters, such as the Hubble constant, and propose a method for doing so by comparing the redshifted memory wedges observed by multiple detectors.

In a self-gravitating scalar field model, we examine how the spin of the central object affects the stability of the field in the presence of superradiant instabilities. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the spin of the central object can significantly impact the growth rate of the unstable modes, with faster-spinning objects resulting in more rapid growth. Additionally, the spin of the object influences the location of the unstable modes in frequency space, with some modes shifting towards the real frequency axis as the object's spin increases. However, this effect is limited, and the unstable modes never become stable, even for rapidly spinning objects. Furthermore, we find that the spin of the object can alter the structure of the unstable configurations, with some modes transitioning from being localized around the object's horizon to being localized around the object's boson cloud as the object's spin increases. These findings have important implications for the detection of superradiant instabilities through gravitational wave observations, with the ability to distinguish between black holes and other compact objects that can support massive scalar fields.

We establish the well-posedness of this Dirichlet problem for a broad class of elliptic operators in divergence form, under minimal assumptions on the coefficients, provided that the Sobolev space parameter $p$ is strictly greater than 1.  Our approach involves proving optimal $L^p$ estimates for the gradient of solutions, which hold for all functions in the kernel of the adjoint operator with the trace of their restriction to the boundary belonging to the space $L^p(\partial\Omega)$.  This result is of particular interest as it allows us to solve the Dirichlet problem in the interior of $\Omega$ for functions $f$ on the boundary that are not in $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ but in the Besov space $\mathcal{B}^{1/p}_{p,p}(\partial\Omega)$, which is the trace space of the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$.

The SunCones project, a multi-messenger study, aims to explore the interplay between cosmic rays, gravitational waves, and other phenomena by studying the impact of dark matter sub-halos on major astrophysical events.  Sub-halos containing massive concentrations of dark matter can distort the light from distant supernovae, resulting in brightening and distortion patterns.  These sub-halos can also trigger other events, such as the merging of supermassive black holes, which can be detected by gravitational wave detectors.  The SunCones project aims to create a comprehensive catalogue of these events over a five-year period, using the data from Euclid and other observatories.  By correlating the data from Euclid with the catalogs from gravitational wave detectors, we can pinpoint the sub-halos responsible for these events and map out the distribution of dark matter in the universe's large-scale structure.  The SunCones project will be able to detect sub-halos with masses as low as $10^9 M_{\odot}$ within Euclid's five-year field of view, providing valuable insights into the universe's dark matter content.

able Artificial Intelligence (XAI) poses a significant challenge in preserving the local feature importance of machine learning models.  Our research indicates that any method capable of accurately approximating feature importance for any possible query within a dataset must compromise DP guarantees.  Furthermore, we prove that any DP-compliant algorithm for local feature importance must incur an error that grows exponentially with the number of features being evaluated.  To address this issue, we propose a novel algorithm for local feature importance that achieves a polynomial approximation within the bounds established in our theoretical findings.  This algorithm, which is based on a randomized feature selection process, can be efficiently executed in a time frame proportional to the logarithm of the number of features.  Our method has been tested on real-world datasets and has been found to produce feature importance scores that are comparable to those generated by state-of-the-art XAI tools.

Notably, the spin hopping between unit cells is influenced by the product of the two dimer bonds that connect them, resulting in an effective t-J-like Hamiltonian with significant modulation. highly energetic events that release vast amounts of energy in gamma rays, often accompanied by afterglows and radio emissions.  The energy released in GRBs is typically concentrated in a relativistic outflow, which can be observed through various wavelengths.  The composition of this outflow is a subject of ongoing debate, with implications for the behavior of the burst and its afterglows.  The presence of heavy elements in the outflow can lead to the formation of heavy ion absorption lines, which can provide valuable insights into the burst's properties.  In this study, we present a theoretical model that predicts the formation of highly ionized iron absorption lines in the optical/UV range of GRB spectra, and we demonstrate that these lines can be detected in the afterglows of GRBs with dense, electron-poor outflows.  Our model also suggests that these absorption lines can be used to estimate the composition of the GRB outflow, and we discuss the potential implications of this discovery for our understanding of these energetic events.

  We first establish that an optimal active learner can achieve the same reward as one without data collection.

  training separate models for each user. In contrast, this paper introduces
  a novel technique called the Personalized Gradient Descent (PGD) algorithm,
  which enables a single model to be trained that can cater to multiple users.
  The pgd algorithm is an adaptation of the gradient descent method, which
  leverages a single shared model for all users while allowing for individual
  model customization through offset parameters. The algorithm updates both
  the shared model and the user-specific offsets using the same training data,
  effectively balancing the needs of individual users and the overall model's
  generalizability. Theoretical analysis shows that the pgd algorithm converges
  to a stationary point of an objective function that combines the users'
  individual model performance with a regularization term that penalizes
  differences between the shared model and the user-specific models. The
  effectiveness of the pgd algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on
  real-world datasets, which reveal its potential for improving the performance
  of machine learning models in a range of applications.

These transients are found in distant galaxies and are believed to be powered by the interaction between compact objects and their surrounding gas clouds. We present a comprehensive spectral and temporal analysis of a specific FXRT, designated as PG 1245+47, which was discovered in a galaxy at a distance of 0.093 from Earth.  This analysis, based on X-ray data from the Swift satellite, reveals that the source's spectrum is best explained by a model of an accreting compact object, which is surrounded by a dense gas cloud.  The model also suggests that the source's central compact object is a stellar-mass black hole, which is accreting matter at a rate of 0.01 times the Eddington limit.  Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the source's flaring activity is characterized by a complex interplay between hard X-ray emission from the compact object and softer X-ray emission from the surrounding gas cloud.

This paper investigates the distribution of sums of independent random variables, denoted as $X_n$, which are uniformly distributed over the integers from 1 to $g$.  It is shown that for a given integer $g$, the probability of $X_n$ taking a specific value $g_j$ in base $g$ is equivalent to the probability of $||n||$ taking the same value.  Consequently, the distribution of $||n||$ can be understood by examining the distribution of $X_n$.  This connection enables us to derive various properties of $||n||$, such as its asymptotic behavior, expected values, and variances.  Additionally, it is demonstrated that the distribution of $||n||$ is independent of the base $g$ used to represent the integers.

data in MRI poses a significant
  challenge, as it is an ill-posed inverse problem.  MRI reconstruction methods
  can be broadly classified into linear and non-linear approaches.  While linear
  techniques are computationally efficient, they often fail to preserve image
  details.  In contrast, non-linear methods, such as deep learning-based models,
  are capable of producing high-quality images but are computationally expensive
  and time-consuming.  To address this issue, we propose a novel method that
  combines the efficiency of linear techniques with the high-quality results of
  non-linear approaches.  Our proposed method, known as the Non-linear Residual
  Estimation (NRE) method, estimates the high-quality under-sampled image
  directly from the under-sampled data and the high-resolution fully-sampled
  image, which is obtained from the under-sampled data via Fourier transform.
  By estimating the residual between the under-sampled image and the fully-sampled
  image, NRE can achieve high-quality reconstructions with fewer acceleration
  factors.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of NRE through numerical simulations
  and MRI experiments, showing that it can accurately reconstruct images with
  up to 6x acceleration, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Existing methods for this task can be broadly classified into two categories: those relying on manually annotated masks and those employing weak supervision.  In this paper, we propose a new camouflaging strategy called Object-Background Swapping (OBS), which is a weak-supervision data annotation method that is simpler to implement than mask-based labeling.  OBS is a time-efficient and cost-effective labeling technique that is easier to apply in practice.  We demonstrate the efficacy of OBS as a weak supervision data annotation method by employing it to create a new camouflaged object detection dataset, the OBS-COD dataset.  This dataset is created by systematically swapping foreground and background objects in images, a process that is both straightforward to implement and can be automated.  We further show that OBS-COD is a valuable resource for the COD community, as it is the first camouflaged object detection dataset annotated using a weak supervision method.  We also show that OBS-COD can be used to train and evaluate camouflaged object detection models, and that these models can be easily adapted to new objects and backgrounds. We analyze the behavior of a particle at the boundary over a long period, observing how it responds to a temporary change in the tree's root structure.  By examining the expected distance the particle has moved from its starting point after a prolonged period, we can identify distinct phases based on the exclusion rate lambda.  For low rates, the expected distance grows linearly with time, while for higher rates, it slows down, mirroring the behavior seen in a standard tree.  This change occurs at a critical rate lambda_c that decreases as the tree's branching factor increases, ultimately approaching zero as the tree's structure becomes more like a standard tree.

characterized by irregular bronchial wall thickness, is a common feature of COPD.  This condition is associated with airflow limitation and chronic inflammation, which can lead to severe complications and significantly impact a patient's quality of life.  Despite its prevalence, airway dilatation is often overlooked in the diagnosis and management of COPD.  This article provides an in-depth examination of the causes, types, diagnosis, and management of airway dilatation in COPD patients.   consisting of a black hole and a neutron star, specifically focusing on cases

  of our results for the detection of these binary systems with gravitational
  wave observatories.
